$comment: Pinned repo-side contract for the controls that would otherwise trust a
repository-controlled artifact at its word.
The rubric invokes package.json scripts, reads facetheory.lesser.json, and runs a
named set of security tests. Every one of those is editable in the same pull
request as the change being gated, so 'the command exited 0' is not by itself
evidence: a script rewritten to `true` exits 0, an emptied test file exits 0, and a
retargeted manifest path exits 0. This file is the expected value each of those
controls asserts against.
What this does buy: a bypass can no longer hide inside an application-shaped file.
Stubbing `pnpm run build` now requires editing gov-infra/planning in the same diff,
at the governance boundary, where the change is the review's subject rather than
incidental. What it does NOT buy: this is not a cryptographic binding, and an
author who edits both sides can still move the pin. The control it composes with is
cross-client adversarial review of the gov-infra diff, not this file alone.
Command text is not behaviour. `validate:csp` pinned to `node scripts/audit-csp.mjs`
holds perfectly while that file is emptied, and SEC-4 then exits 0 having audited
nothing. So the pins below reach content: every executable this rubric runs, and
every probe it counts, is bound by SHA-256 rather than by the string that names it.
Changing any value here is a governance change. It travels with the reason, in the
commit that needs it, and never as drive-by maintenance. Duplicate keys are rejected
when this file is read: JSON.parse is last-wins, so a repeated key is a value a
reviewer reads and a different value a control enforces.
Exact expected text of every script the rubric's exit-code trust depends on,
including the transitive closure reached through `pnpm run`. CON-5 asserts each
pinned script matches byte-for-byte, and that no pinned script delegates to a
script outside this map — a sub-script is otherwise a hole under a pinned parent.

expected.build:assets: node scripts/copy-facetheory-manifest.mjs && node scripts/build-stylesheet.mjs && node scripts/copy-brand-assets.mjs
expected.build: pnpm run typecheck && pnpm run svelte-check && pnpm run build:client && pnpm run build:server && pnpm run build:assets && pnpm run validate
expected.validate: pnpm run validate:graphql && pnpm run validate:renderer-authority && pnpm run validate:csp && pnpm run validate:seam-graph

$comment: The content of everything the guarded scripts above actually execute. CON-5 walks
the closure — each `node <path>` target, each file a listed glob expands to, and
each relative module those files import, transitively — and asserts a SHA-256 for
every member. A target with no pin fails; a pin no command reaches fails too, so
this map stays exactly the closure instead of drifting into a wish list.
`unpinned_import_roots` is the declared boundary of that walk. `src/` is the
application the probes are written against: hashing it would freeze the subject
under governance and invert the relationship, because the probe is the gate and the
module is what it judges. `build/` is generated output — regenerated every run, and
asserted by COM-1 and driven by SEC-6 rather than pinned. A gate that imports helper
logic out of either root is a limit recorded in the threat model, not a hole this
map closes.
`allowed_globs` is the set of glob arguments a guarded `node` invocation may pass.
Every file a listed glob expands to still has to be pinned; the list exists so a
new glob is a governance edit rather than a silent widening.
`node gov-infra/verifiers/check-package-scripts.mjs --print-hashes` prints this map
for the current tree, so a legitimate move is mechanical rather than hand-computed.
TWO gov-infra FILES ARE PINNED HERE, which is a governance decision rather than an
oversight. `tests/con5-import-reader.test.mjs` runs this control's own verifier over
a synthetic tree, so that verifier — and `strict-json.mjs`, which it imports — are
code a guarded command executes, and this map's whole claim is that such code is
bound. They were exempted until round 9 on the ground that the parent stages gov-infra
and `packDigest` in `gov-infra/pack.json` binds it; the review established that no
local control verifies that digest and that this verifier's bytes moved in this pull
request while `pack.json` did not. Recomputing `packDigest` needs the pack's inventory
and algorithm, which this repository does not hold — that control belongs to the
parent's staging discipline and is routed there. The accepted cost of the local one:
a parent restage turns CON-5 red until these two pins move, which is a recorded event
being re-acknowledged rather than a gate breaking.
`unfollowable_loads_disclosed` is the third boundary, and the one no reading can
close. Three shapes land here. A load whose TARGET is an expression —
`import(pathToFileURL(x).href)` — names a module nothing static can follow. A load
whose LOADER is a construction the reading does not model — an aliased `require`,
`module.require`, a destructured `{ require: r }`, `eval`, `new Function`, a
`node:vm` import — reaches a file the walk never sees. And an EXECUTION facility —
`spawn`, `exec`, `fork`, a `Worker`, `process.dlopen`, `WebAssembly` — starts code
running that this process never loaded at all. Every one of them is a place the walk
stops with something unpinned beyond it. CON-5 used to be silent about all three
because its reader could not see them, and silence and permission are the same green.
Each site is declared here with the line it sits on and its reason. An undisclosed
one is a finding; a disclosure matching no site in the closure is a finding too;
and one declaration binds ONE load, so two identical calls need two entries and a
repeated entry is rejected outright. The line costs nothing to maintain that the
pin does not already cost — the file's own SHA-256 below has to move in the same
diff whenever the line does, and that pin is what binds these sites: no load can
appear, move or change without a governance edit in the same diff.
`binds` is the optional half that turns a report into a binding, and the reason the
execution shape is disclosable rather than banned. A site that runs a REPOSITORY
file names it there, and CON-5 admits that path to the closure exactly as it admits
an import: pinned, hashed, and walked for its own imports in turn — so rewriting the
file the site runs turns this control red. A site that runs the system `git` binary,
or a build artifact, or bytes the probe has just written to a temp directory, omits
`binds` and says so in its reason. A path under a declared unpinned root is refused
there, because a `binds` that pins no bytes reads as coverage and is not. The choice
is written down here rather than inferred from a walk that stopped, which is the
whole point of the list.
AND A `binds` IS CHECKED AGAINST ITS OWN SITE, which round 9 added because the list
was previously admitted at its word. A declaration bound a pinned file while the
`spawnSync` on the line it declared executed a different, unpinned one, and CON-5 was
green with that decoy rewritten wholesale — a pin pointed away from the file that
runs, which is the round-7 failure moved out of the resolver and into this file,
where it reads as coverage more loudly because a human wrote the path down. So the
reading reports the literals each site is written to hand its facility, and the
repository files among them must be exactly what `binds` names: one the site runs and
the declaration misses is a finding, and one the declaration names and the site does
not run is a finding too. Spelling does not decide it — `./x`, `x` and `a/../x` are
normalised to one path before anything is compared.
What a `binds` cannot do is excuse a target no reading can see. Where the path is an
argv element or a constant declared elsewhere, there is no literal to check the claim
against, so the site is carried by its REASON rather than by a pin nothing compares
to anything. The practical rule for an author is short: write the path where you run
it, and then bind it.

unfollowable_loads_disclosed.reason: Runs only the system `pnpm`, `lesser`, and `curl` binaries from the closed deployment plan assembled in this pinned file. No repository file is handed directly to `spawn`: pnpm's repository script delegation remains separately pinned by package_scripts.expected and this executable closure, while the three executable binaries are operator-installed PATH dependencies outside any repo-local hash boundary.

Loads build/server/handler.mjs with the same query suffix lesser's client_ssr_host wrapper appends, which is the regression probe for the double-instantiation defect that 500'd every context-using route. `build/` is a declared unpinned root — generated output asserted by COM-1 and driven by SEC-6 — and the suffixed specifier is assembled at run time rather than written.

Runs this control's own verifier over a synthetic three-file repository in a temp directory — the only way to assert what CON-5 does with a tree, since it takes its root from `process.cwd()`. The verifier IS bound: `binds` names it, so it is pinned, hashed and walked for its own imports like any other file a guarded command executes, and the path is spelled as a literal at the call so that claim is checkable against the site. The previous entry exempted it instead, on the ground that gov-infra is genome content the parent stages and `packDigest` in `gov-infra/pack.json` binds. Round 9's review refuted that: `packDigest` appears nowhere in this repository but in the file that declares it, no local control recomputes or verifies it, and the pack's file inventory and digest algorithm are not available here to build one — so this verifier's bytes changed in this very pull request while `pack.json` did not move. Verifying `packDigest` belongs to the parent's staging discipline and is routed there; the strongest LOCAL control is the one every other executable in this closure already has, and it is applied here. The cost is real and accepted: a parent restage of the pack turns CON-5 red until this pin moves. A restage is a recorded event, and a pin that forces it to be re-acknowledged is the honest behaviour — an exemption resting on a digest nothing checks is not.

Runs `scripts/audit-renderer-authority.mjs` in a child process, which is how this probe asserts the audit’s exit code and output rather than its internals. The target is a repository file written as a literal, so it is bound: `binds` admits it to the closure, and it carries a pinned SHA-256 like any import.

No repository file is executed: `git` is resolved on PATH and its bytes are the operating system's, outside any repo-local hash boundary.

Runs the system `git` binary for the same tracked-file listing the gate uses, so the probe asserts the inventory against the same set the gate judges rather than against a directory listing that can differ. No repository file is executed.

Runs the system `git` binary to list a directory's tracked files, NUL-separated and rooted with `-C`, which is the reading three probes share so none of them lists a directory a concurrent probe is planting fixtures in. No repository file is executed.

$comment: `build.command` is what `lesser client install` executes. An allowlist of exact
invocations is the only form of this check that means anything: any non-empty
string array satisfies a shape check, including one that runs something else
entirely. Path keys are validated structurally (no absolute path, no `..`,
resolved beneath the repository root, entry beneath the server dir) rather than
pinned, so the layout can move without a governance edit while containment holds.
SEC-6's inventory. `node --test <files>` exits 0 on a file containing no tests,
so existence is not coverage. Each file below must be present and must report at
least `min_test_points` passing TAP test points (TAP's own name for the ok/not ok
assertions a run emits, counting nested subtests). Deleting a test, emptying a
file, or dropping one from the invocation all fail the control.
The minimums sit at the current counts. They ratchet up with new coverage and
are lowered only with a stated reason — lowering one is how coverage is retired,
and it is meant to be visible when it happens.
A count is still not coverage: sixteen assertions that assert nothing satisfy a
minimum of sixteen, and one probe symlinked to another satisfies two entries from
one file. So each entry pins the probe's SHA-256 as well, symlinked probes are
rejected on lstat, and two entries naming one path are rejected outright.
The hard boundary is that no install in this rubric or in CI runs lifecycle
scripts: every `pnpm install` carries `--ignore-scripts`. The scans below are
heuristic screening layered on top of that boundary, never a substitute for it.
`--ignore-scripts` does NOT disable pnpm's own `.pnpmfile.cjs` hooks, so their
presence is a finding in its own right unless disclosed here. `onlyBuiltDependencies`
is pnpm 10's opt-back-in for lifecycle scripts and is likewise a finding unless
disclosed. Both lists are empty: contentus runs no install-time code.
Binds the two greater channels to each other and to a named release, rather than
to a shape. A 40-hex-shaped ref is not evidence of anything: every commit in every
repository is 40 hex. `vendored_ref` is the greater-components commit the
greater-v0.13.2 vendoring came from, recorded at the audit-remediation `greater
update` run — the release named in `release_tag` beside it, which is the only pin
this block asserts.
Both values move together at a CLI pin bump and only through the CLI.
`cli_version` is the version string the CLI must print; a digest-verified install
at any other version FAILS SEC-7 rather than reporting on a tree it does not match.
`cli_asset` is the provenance of the tool itself. The CLI is not on the npm
registry, so nothing about the downloaded bytes is checked by a package manager,
and `--version` is the tool describing itself — any executable can print `0.13.0`
and emit a plausible doctor document. The installer verifies this digest before
unpacking and SEC-7 re-verifies it at gate time. A PATH `greater` is not accepted
at all: unverifiable provenance is BLOCKED, never PASS.

one is the evidence that it was not casual:

(`Review.QueueCard`, `Review.AttributionStrip`, `Review.VerdictActions`) is a
`review` registry entry that exists only from greater-v0.12.0, so `greater add
review` at the old pin does not resolve at all.

`Message.svelte` sanitizing and rendering declaratively, `Conversations.svelte`

It also retired the `ws` advisory (GHSA-96hv-2xvq-fx4p) from the SEC-2 disclosed
set, because 0.13.0's adapters resolve ws@8.21.0.

One consumption of the raw field remains: contentus's own
`toVerdictRecord` (src/lib/cms/review-contract.ts, ~line 421) still

CON-4 forces the rest, at every bump: each `installed[]` entry must carry
`vendored_ref`, so the whole vendored tree and every tarball pin move together, in
one commit, through the CLI. The alternative — hand-copying components — is the
vendored-source edit this repository refuses outright.
Least-privilege GitHub Actions permissions. Every workflow must declare an
explicit top-level `permissions:` block, and every scope in it — top-level or
job-level — must be `read` or `none`, except the exact write grants listed here.
CodeQL's `security-events: write` is the one exception: uploading a SARIF result
requires it, and the alternative is not running CodeQL.
`allowed_install_invocations` is the exact set of package-manager installs any
workflow — or any local composite action a workflow reaches — may run. The whole
supply-chain claim rests on `--ignore-scripts`, and the rubric can only ever fix
its own install: the workflow installs run before the rubric starts, so dropping
the flag from one of them executes dependency lifecycle code and the rubric then
reports green on the tree that code produced. The greater CLI no longer appears
here because it installs through `node gov-infra/verifiers/install-greater-cli.mjs`,
which verifies the release-asset digest first and passes `--ignore-scripts` itself.
`pinned_run_scripts` is what makes the workflow scanner's appearance rule usable.
Event-derived data may appear in a `run:` script in two shapes only: argv to a
script pinned below, or an argument to printf after a literal format. Everything
else is a finding — `bash -c`, a `<(…)` operand, a heredoc body, a `read` carrier,
the argv of any command that is not one of these scripts. Four rounds of naming
execution positions each lost to a shell spelling they had not enumerated, so the
rule stopped asking what a position would do.
The pin is the allowance. A script whose file is missing, is a symlink, or does not
hash to the value below is not in the verified set, and a `run:` handing event data
to it is judged as an ordinary command — a finding. That is also what binds the
behaviour these two workflows used to spell out inline: `main-guard`'s three `test`
comparisons and DCO's commit walk are now content-bound here rather than matched as
command text, while MAI-4 still binds the exact invocation in the workflow.
